entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Sunpadh, an Iranian nobleman from the ancient House of Karen, ignited a formidable, albeit short-lived, uprising against the newly established Abbasid Caliphate in northern Iran between 755 and 756 CE. Emerging in the immediate aftermath of the assassination of Abu Muslim al-Khorasani, the revered general who had brought the Abbasids to power, Sunpadh's rebellion tapped into deep-seated Iranian national sentiment, a desire for autonomy, and a lingering reverence for pre-Islamic Persian traditions, challenging the nascent caliphate's authority at its very foundation. His movement, rooted in Tabaristan and extending its influence to Rey, aimed to avenge Abu Muslim and potentially restore a Persian kingdom.

Following Abu Muslim's murder by Caliph al-Mansur in 755 CE, Sunpadh rallied a coalition of disaffected Iranian elements, including Zoroastrians and adherents of various Mazdakite-influenced sects. He declared his intention to march on Baghdad to avenge Abu Muslim, whom he claimed was not dead but merely in hiding and would return as a messianic figure. Sunpadh's forces swiftly captured Rey (modern Tehran province), a strategically vital city, and even began minting coins in his own name, signifying a direct challenge to Abbasid sovereignty. This rapid expansion alarmed the Caliphate, prompting a decisive military response under the command of Jahwar ibn Marrar al-Ijli.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Sunpadh's rebellion, though short-lived, was a major challenge to the nascent Abbasid Caliphate, demonstrating persistent Iranian resistance and contributing to the complex political landscape of early Islamic Persia. It underscored the fragile nature of Abbasid authority outside of Iraq and the enduring appeal of pre-Islamic traditions among local populations.
